channel.title: California Uzbek — Latest
channel.description: Independent analysis · Central Asia & world geopolitics

item.title: About 300 migrants cross into Mexico and set off for the US; Trump warns of tariffs
item.description: A group that crossed from Guatemala into Chiapas on 20 November plans to join a 1,500-strong caravan; migrants hope for relief after the midterms, while the US says policy is unchanged.

item.title: Croatia recruits Uzbek construction workers: €1,000 net salary and free housing
item.description: Uzbekistan's Migration Agency has posted five construction vacancies — €1,000 net a month, free accommodation and an €80 monthly meal allowance; applications close on 1 December.

item.title: Trump, Xi and Putin meet in Shenzhen: the first-ever trilateral nuclear summit
item.description: On 19 November the leaders of three nuclear powers sat at one table for the first time; they issued a joint statement rejecting nuclear war, but signed no concrete arms-cut deal.

item.title: Russia's military cargo ship 'Sparta II' set ablaze by drones in the Gulf of Finland
item.description: On 21 November a sanctioned Russian ship bound for Kaliningrad was struck by two drones in international waters; it drifted into Finnish waters, with no casualties and no claim of responsibility.

item.title: Uzbekistan's banks turn to AI: SQB built its own platform in just 6 months
item.description: At the third FINNEXT Asia forum in Tashkent on November 19, some 700 financiers gathered. SQB put its SQB.NOVA AI platform into production in six months, while an Islamic banking law took effect on June 29 — verified facts only.

item.title: Primary, secondary and anonymous sources: how to judge a news report
item.description: In a stream of news, not every source carries the same weight. This guide explains the difference between primary and secondary sources, and between named and anonymous sources, strictly on the facts. The aim is to help the reader see what a report actually rests on. All definitions draw on academic libraries and journalism codes of ethics.

item.title: Uzbekistan's accession to GUUAM (1999) and its withdrawal (2005)
item.description: In its first decade of independence, Uzbekistan tried several foreign-policy directions. One of them was GUUAM — a post-Soviet grouping Uzbekistan joined in 1999 and left in 2005. This facts-only guide traces that episode step by step, from joining to withdrawal. The map above is a general illustration of the post-Soviet (CIS) geopolitical blocs — the Russia-led CSTO and GUAM — and reflects the situation after Uzbekistan's 2005 withdrawal.

item.title: Malaysia's Rohingya: 133,000 refugees, but without the right to work or legal status
item.description: Malaysia has long been a haven for Rohingya Muslims, but because it has not signed the Refugee Convention they cannot legally work; in 2026 hate speech and pressure to return have intensified.

item.title: US court: agriculture secretary's religious emails likely crossed constitutional boundaries
item.description: A federal judge in California issued a preliminary injunction, finding that Secretary Brooke Rollins's Christian holiday emails to roughly 100,000 USDA staff likely violated the First Amendment's Establishment Clause.

item.title: Kyrgyzstan proposes visa-free entry for 18 more countries and 60-day stays
item.description: Kyrgyzstan's tourism agency has opened a draft resolution for consultation that would add 18 countries to the visa-free list and extend the permitted visa-free stay from 30 to 60 days within a 120-day period.

item.title: Israel strikes southern Lebanon again as drones fly over Beirut and Sidon
item.description: On 20 November Israel carried out airstrikes on Kfar Tebnit and shelled several villages; a day earlier it said it had struck a Hezbollah weapons site in eastern Lebanon. No casualties were reported.

item.title: How personal bankruptcy works in the US: Chapter 7 and Chapter 13
item.description: Bankruptcy is a federal court process for individuals in the US who can no longer pay their debts. There are two main types: Chapter 7 (discharging debt by selling property) and Chapter 13 (a 3–5 year repayment plan). This guide explains the difference between them, the "means test," which debts are not dischargeable, the impact on credit history, and key points for immigrants — based solely on official sources. This is general information, not legal advice.

item.title: The Mennonites' "Great Trek" to Central Asia (1880–1884): the Ak Metchet community near Khiva
item.description: German-speaking Mennonite Christians trekked some 3,000 km across the steppe into Central Asia in 1880–1884. The migration had two causes: the end of their exemption from military service, and the preacher Claas Epp Jr.'s prophecy of the Second Coming of Christ. In 1884, at the invitation of the Khan of Khiva, Muhammad Rahim Khan II, Epp and his followers founded the village of Ak Metchet near Khiva. The community farmed, practiced fine crafts, and introduced photography; it was here that Khudaybergen Divanov learned to take photographs. Ak Metchet remained the last independent Mennonite community in the Soviet Union until its deportation to Tajikistan in 1935.

item.title: New report: state-imposed forced labor persists in Uzbekistan's silk sector
item.description: Drawing on 85 interviews across 21 districts, the Uzbek Forum for Human Rights found the state still sets cocoon quotas and prices, with farmers who refuse facing threats.

item.title: Uzbekistan aims for $10,000 GDP per capita within 4–5 years
item.description: Central Bank Deputy Chairman Nodirbek Ochilov announced the goal at an IMF presentation; the current figure is about $3,846.

item.title: Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan discuss restoring visa-free travel for border residents
item.description: Tashkent–Ashgabat flights and a three-day visa-free regime for border-area residents — the two states want to return to a 2004 agreement. Direct flights have been halted since 2013.

item.title: The Turkestani political diaspora during the Cold War (1950–1990): organizations, press and radio in the West
item.description: After World War II a community of Turkestani political émigrés formed in the West — mainly West Germany (Munich), Turkey (Istanbul) and later the United States. It was made up of pre-war émigrés, former POWs and veterans of the Turkestan Legion. The community's central voice became Radio Liberty, broadcast from Munich; scholars such as Baymirza Hayit wrote the history of Turkestan. This facts-only history presents the subject's contested aspects with sourced attribution.

item.title: Mosque set on fire in northern Israel; politicians call it a 'hate crime'
item.description: The lower part of a mosque in the village of al-Dahi was set alight and 'revenge' graffiti was sprayed nearby; police and the Shin Bet opened an investigation.

item.title: Advertising, sponsored and 'native' content: how to tell paid material from independent journalism
item.description: In modern feeds and news sites, paid material often appears disguised as an ordinary article, review or post — this is called 'native' advertising. Under the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC), an ad must be identifiable as advertising to consumers, and a material connection (payment, a gift) must be disclosed. This facts-only guide explains sponsored content, advertorials, influencer and affiliate marketing, and gives practical tests for separating paid material from independent journalism.

item.title: Emergency medical help in the USA: how 911, ambulances, the ER and urgent care work
item.description: In the US, calling 911 in an emergency is free from any phone, and by law the Emergency Room (ER) must screen and stabilize anyone — regardless of citizenship or ability to pay (EMTALA, 1986). But the ambulance is not free and an uninsured ER visit is expensive. This facts-only guide explains 911 and 988, the difference between the ER and urgent care, the costs, and practical rules for immigrants.

item.title: ICJ: Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslims
item.description: The UN's top court ruled 9 votes to 6 in a landmark judgment; the decision is final and cannot be appealed.

item.title: Alisher Qodirov proposes that children in Uzbek families be educated in the state language
item.description: The leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party wants to amend Article 38 of the Preschool Education Law to limit the language of early education to the state language for children of Uzbek parents. The restriction would not apply to higher education or to ethnic minorities.

item.title: German company offers nursing jobs to Uzbek citizens with salaries up to €2,050
item.description: Bildung & Beruf GmbH has posted 24 vacancies in neurology and stroke care; the requirements include B1 German and two years of experience, with applications due by 20 November.

item.title: Uzbekistan's 1996 currency crisis and the restriction of som convertibility (1996–2003)
item.description: After the som was introduced in 1994, a poor 1996 cotton harvest and dwindling reserves caused a balance-of-payments crisis. That year Uzbekistan restricted foreign-exchange trading, halted som convertibility, and its IMF program broke down. The result was a multiple exchange-rate system that lasted years, with a large gap between the official and black-market rates. Only on 15 October 2003 did Uzbekistan accept IMF Article VIII obligations — current-account convertibility. This history is facts only.

item.title: UN's top court finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya
item.description: The International Court of Justice ruled 9–6 that Myanmar committed genocide in northern Rakhine — the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide by the ICJ.

item.title: Cyber fraudsters stole 278.3 billion soums from Uzbeks in nine months
item.description: Between 1 January and 1 October 2026, more than 39,000 fraud cases were recorded in Uzbekistan, costing citizens 278.3 billion soums. Prompt action blocked 113.1 billion soums.

item.title: COVID-19 and 2020: the mass return of Uzbek labor migrants
item.description: The 2020 pandemic triggered one of the sharpest crises in the history of Uzbek labor migration. Borders closed, thousands of migrants were stranded at the Kazakh border, and — according to a UN Development Programme survey — about half a million Uzbeks returned home over the year. Remittances suffered, by the World Bank's assessment, their sharpest fall since independence. A historical reference, facts only.

item.title: Iran says it struck a US radar in Bahrain; the US denies it
item.description: The IRGC announced it had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain; US Central Command said two drones were shot down and nothing was damaged. Iran called it a response to a strike on Sirik.

item.title: Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan sign an agreement to protect the saiga
item.description: A memorandum signed on the sidelines of COP31 in Antalya covers joint monitoring of migration routes, habitat restoration and anti-poaching; Kazakhstan's saiga population reached around 4.7 million in 2026.

item.title: How government (national) debt works: deficits, bonds, and the debt-to-GDP ratio
item.description: A budget deficit is a single year's shortfall (spending exceeds revenue); national debt is the accumulated total of those deficits over the years. Governments borrow mainly by issuing bonds (government securities); debt is measured against gross domestic product (GDP). For reference: per the IMF, Uzbekistan's public debt was 32.6% of GDP at the end of 2024. A reference, facts only.
